queries.hook: I feel guilty about something I did. Inside, I keep going over it again and again, and I don't know how to carry it.

queries.act: Be on your own side: lift yourself up, make amends where you can, and begin again; no one who does good is lost.

verse.why: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.

prasang.title: What makes an action happen
prasang.summary: Every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. Seeing oneself as the only doer is a mistake.
prasang.lesson: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, right after he explained that every action has five causes. Krishna warns against the mistake of seeing yourself as the only cause. If you think you alone made something succeed or fail, you are missing the whole picture. You are one of five factors, not the entire story.
verse.for_you: You are holding the whole weight of this moment on your own shoulders, replaying it because you believe you alone caused the harm. You are one cause among the five, and that is your part to own. You are not the whole picture.
verse.try_today: Notice one factor outside your control in this memory.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the crossroads where your part ends and the rest begins.
asks: How do I stop being the only cause in my mind?
What are the other four causes I am ignoring?
Is my guilt the whole picture?

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: Rama, near the end of his lament, says where the real enemy lives.
verse.sanskrit: शत्रवश्चेन्द्रियाण्येव सत्यं यातमसत्यताम् । प्रहरत्यात्मनैवात्मा मनसैव मनो रिपुः ॥
verse.line: No one hurts us like we hurt ourselves. The mind becomes the mind's own enemy.
verse.translation: Our own senses are the enemies; truth itself has turned untrue; the self strikes the self, and the mind is the mind's own enemy.
verse.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
verse.misuse: Not a reason to blame yourself. Vasishtha's answer is that the same mind can lift itself.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

verse.meaning: Rama, in his deepest despair, tells the sages where the real trouble lives. He says our own senses are the enemies. Truth itself has turned untrue. The self strikes the self. The mind becomes the mind's own enemy. He is not naming an outside villain. He is naming the pattern of how we turn on ourselves when we feel empty. The mind is not the answer yet. It is the question. It is the thing that hurts itself, and that is the first thing to see honestly.
verse.for_you: You keep going over what you did. You hold yourself to a standard you would never give a friend. That is the self striking the self. The mind becomes the mind's own enemy when it rehearses the same regret. You do not need to fix the past today.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind starts rehearsing the regret. Just name it.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own lament, and the enemy is the one you are arguing with.
asks: Where does the self strike the self in my own story?
How do I stop rehearsing the wound?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse.sanskrit: श्री भगवानुवाचपार्थ नैवेह नामुत्र विनाशस्तस्य विद्यते । नहि कल्याणकृत्कश्चिद्दुर्गतिं तात गच्छति ॥
verse.line: Whoever does good never comes to ruin, my friend. Not here, not after.
verse.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Partha, there is no ruin for him either in this world or the next. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to grief.
verse.why: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

prasang.title: What becomes of one who falls from yoga
prasang.summary: Arjuna fears that one who falls short is lost like a torn cloud. Krishna promises that no one who does good comes to ruin; past effort carries forward and they strive again.
prasang.lesson: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that no sincere effort ever comes to ruin. Arjuna has asked what happens to someone who tries and fails. Krishna answers that a person who does good is never lost. The effort is not wasted. It carries forward into the next attempt. This means that a fall does not erase what came before it. The path simply continues from where it left off.
verse.for_you: You are holding a standard that crushes you. The guilt is not a verdict on you. It is a sign that you care about doing right. What you did was not the end of your story. The effort you put in before still matters.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing you did right today.
verse.scene_line: You are standing in the gap between what you did and what you hoped to do.
asks: What if my effort was not wasted?
How do I start again without shame?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: What falls away for one who knows that joy.
verse.sanskrit: एतꣳह वाव न तपति । किमहꣳसाधु नाकरवम् । किमहं पापमकरवमिति ।
verse.line: Free in that joy, one no longer agonises: 'Why didn't I do right? Why did I do wrong?'
verse.translation: Such a one is no longer tormented by the thought: why did I not do good? Why did I do wrong?
verse.why: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.
verse.misuse: Not a licence to stop caring about harm done; it frees you from self-torment so you can make amends.

prasang.title: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

verse.meaning: The teacher asks what falls away for one who knows that joy. Free in that joy, one no longer agonises: 'Why didn't I do right? Why did I do wrong?' The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret. It does not mean you stop caring about the harm you caused. It means you are freed from the self-torment that keeps you stuck.
verse.for_you: You keep going over it again and again, as if the loop itself could change the past. The weight of that is real. But the text asks what falls away for one who knows joy. Your work and your guilt are both real.
verse.try_today: Notice when the loop starts, and let the thought pass without feeding it.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own measure of joy, asking what falls away.
asks: How do I separate the fact of my mistake from the story I tell about it?
Can regret exist without the belief that I am not good enough?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
verse.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help'. Arjuna himself asks for help; this is about not abandoning yourself.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.for_you: You are replaying a moment at work, turning it over and over, as if you alone wrote the script and alone must carry the weight. The text asks you to stop treating your own mind as the enemy that must be punished.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of the field, and the only opponent you face is your own reflection.
asks: How do I stop being my own worst enemy?
What does it mean to be my own friend here?
Can I let go of the need to punish myself?

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: यत्कल्याणमभिध्यायेत्तत्रात्मानं नियोजयेत् / न पापं प्रति पापः स्यात्साधुरेव सदा भवेत्
verse.line: Don't become bad because someone was bad to you. Stay good.
verse.translation: Keep your mind on what is good and commit yourself to it. Do not become wicked in return for wickedness; always remain good.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.
verse.misuse: Staying good does not mean staying silent or unprotected.

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.meaning: Dharmavyadha, a meat-seller in Mithila, is speaking to Kaushika, a proud Brahmin ascetic. Kaushika has come seeking wisdom after his own anger destroyed his merit. The butcher tells him to keep his mind on what is good and commit to it. Do not become wicked in return for wickedness. Always remain good.
verse.for_you: The resentment you hold is a kind of wickedness turned inward, and it is exhausting you. You are not obligated to accept the wrong done to you, but you are free to stop letting it make you smaller. Choose to remain good in your own sight, for your own sake.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment you want to return their badness with your own badness, and choose not to.

story.title: Six seekers wait a year
story.story_hook: Six seekers arrived with fuel in their hands and questions on their lips, and were told to wait a year.
story.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.
story.lesson: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.

anchor.speaker: Pippalada
anchor.sanskrit: तेषामसौ विरजो ब्रह्मलोको न येषु जिह्ममनृतं न माया चेति ॥
anchor.line: The pure world belongs to those with no crookedness, no lying and no trickery in them.
anchor.translation: That stainless world of Brahman belongs to those in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood and no deceit.
anchor.why: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.

prasang.title: Six seekers wait a year
prasang.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.
prasang.story_hook: Six seekers arrived with fuel in their hands and questions on their lips, and were told to wait a year.
prasang.lesson: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.

story.hook_title: Six seekers came to a sage with their biggest questions, and he made them wait a year
story.teaser: Six seekers came to a sage with their biggest questions, and he made them wait a year
story.for_you: You have been waiting a long time to be told you are enough, but the truth is, you could sit with yourself first. The seekers who waited a year were not being tested. They were being prepared to hear the truth without running from it.
asks: What would it mean to stop waiting for proof of my worth?
Can I face the year ahead without needing an answer today?
What does it look like to be on my own side?
